opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually one of the most exciting times to enter this field. If you look at what happened with language models, a lot of the foundational questions got answered relatively quickly once we had the data and the compute. Physical AI is different. We're still at a very early stage, and that means there are many open problems where a single researcher or a small team can still make a real contribution.

Take data, for example. For language, we had the internet. For the physical world, we don't have an equivalent. Robots don't generate trillions of tokens of interaction data on their own. So questions like how we use simulation, how we build world models that can generate realistic and physically plausible experiences, and how we transfer from simulation to the real world are all wide open. These aren't just engineering problems. They're deep research questions.

There's also the question of representation. What is the right way to represent the physical world? Is it pixels, 3D structure, physics states, or some learned latent space? We don't have a consensus yet. And then there's reasoning. How does a model understand cause and effect, or predict what happens when you push an object or pour water? That kind of common sense about physics is something humans pick up as infants, and our models still struggle with it.

My advice to young researchers is to not be intimidated by the scale of the big labs. Yes, compute matters, but in a field this young, good ideas still matter enormously. Find a problem you really care about, maybe at the intersection of vision, graphics, and robotics, and go deep. Many breakthroughs in physical AI will come from people who understand both learning and the physical world, like how light works, how materials behave, how contact works. That cross-disciplinary background is a real advantage.

And honestly, the impact is going to be huge. If we get physical AI right, it changes manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, and how we live day to day. So for anyone who wants to work on something meaningful for the next ten or twenty years, I think this is a wonderful place to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses language models and potential impacts of Physical AI, but does not say that advances in AI enable scientific breakthroughs beyond Physical AI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this is one of the most exciting moments to enter the field, honestly. When I started working on generative models, the community was small, and the problems felt very academic. Physical AI is different. It is a convergence of several things that have matured at the same time: large-scale foundation models, simulation and synthetic data, and real hardware that is finally cheap and capable enough to deploy at scale.

For a researcher entering today, I would say the opportunity is that the problem is still wide open. Language models have a fairly established recipe now. In Physical AI we do not yet have that recipe. We do not fully agree on what the right data is, what the right representation of the physical world is, or how a model should reason about physics, about time, about cause and effect. World models are one direction we believe in strongly, but there are still fundamental questions about how to make them accurate, controllable, and efficient enough to actually run on a robot or in a vehicle.

The other thing I would tell young researchers is that this field rewards people who are willing to cross boundaries. You need to understand learning, but also a bit of graphics, a bit of simulation, a bit of control, and you need to care about the system end to end. The people who will make the biggest contributions are the ones who are comfortable going from the model all the way down to the deployment and back.

And the demand is enormous. Every industry that touches the physical world, manufacturing, logistics, transportation, healthcare, is looking for this. So the research you do will not sit in a paper. It will show up in the real world much faster than before. For a researcher, that feedback loop is very motivating. You get to see whether your ideas actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says mature foundation models and other advances create opportunities in Physical AI, but it does not identify scientific breakthroughs beyond Physical AI.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an exciting time to enter Physical AI because there are still so many open questions. The challenge is to build intelligence that can act in the physical world, where actions have consequences and the environment doesn’t always behave the way you expect.

For researchers, that creates opportunities across several areas: learning from limited data, building useful simulations, understanding how to represent the world, and connecting perception with action. How do you learn something in simulation and make it work reliably in a real environment? How do you recognize when your model is uncertain and respond appropriately? Those are rich research problems.

My advice would be to pick a concrete task and work through the whole system. When you actually try to make something work, you discover gaps that aren’t obvious from a benchmark. And those gaps can become very good research questions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open research problems and opportunities within Physical AI, but does not say that AI advances enable scientific breakthroughs beyond Physical AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very exciting time to enter Physical AI, because there are still so many fundamental questions open. How does a system learn about the physical world? How does it connect perception with action? And how do we evaluate whether it can handle a situation it hasn’t seen before?

For researchers, the opportunity is to pick one of those problems and make a meaningful contribution. That could be learning from limited data, building better simulations, or making models more reliable when they interact with the real world. You don’t necessarily have to build an entire robot system to have an impact.

I would encourage people to stay close to experiments. An idea can look very good on a benchmark, but when you put it into a physical system, you discover what you were missing. Those gaps are often where the most interesting research begins.
